notes.3: A significant number of candidates incorrectly chose option D. This was probably based on it being the lightest of the balls.
notes.7: The most popular option was A, implying that candidates had multiplied force by mass to obtain the resultant force, and had then not performed the necessary subtraction.
notes.8: A majority of candidates subtracted the two velocities without taking into account the fact that the final velocity is of the opposite sign to the initial velocity. So they obtained a velocity change of 2 m / s instead of 4 m / s.
notes.10: A significant number of candidates believed that shining a light onto a block of iron does not transfer energy. For that to be true, the block would have to be reflecting the light perfectly, which is impossible. �PAGE�9
notes.11: A significant number of candidates did not notice that the time needed converting to seconds.
notes.12: Although stronger candidates answered this question correctly, many others did not. Candidates needed to know the formula for pressure, and to be careful about the conversion of units.
notes.13: Many candidates thought that the pressure in the Torricellian vacuum is above atmospheric pressure but stronger candidates answered correctly.
notes.19: A large number of candidates did not recognise that atomic vibrations transfer energy to the free electrons and receive it at the destination.
notes.20: Option A was a common incorrect choice, probably because candidates recognised than black surfaces are better emitters than white surfaces. This was in spite of the fact that the question stated that the black surface is emitting less radiation in this case and that conductors of radiation makes no sense in this context.
notes.21: Although stronger candidates answered this correctly, a number of other candidates selected option A.
notes.22: A significant number of candidates forgot to take the sines of the angles.
notes.23: Only stronger candidates answered this correctly. At angles infinitesimally larger than θ, no light will emerge, so this is indeed the critical angle. And since the question declares that there is some light not travelling along the reflection path, it cannot be total internal reflection.
notes.25: Stronger candidates answered correctly. However, a large number of other candidates did not notice the ‘there-and-back’ nature of the situation, and others did not convert from km to m.
notes.27: Candidates were not expected to know any of the relative velocities, but they should know that sound travels considerably faster in solids than in gases or liquids.
notes.28: Nearly as many candidates selected option A as the correct option, B.
notes.30: There was a common belief that positive ions can move around in a metal. It is just the electrons that do the moving.
notes.32: Many candidates found this question challenging. When the resistance of the LDR is low, the p.d. across it is low and vice versa, so that eliminates A and B. Candidates then needed to be clear that, in dim lighting, the LDR’s resistance is high. �PAGE�10
